newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian government calls budget confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Italian government calls budget confidence vote.

text.p: Italy's centre-left government called another confidence vote in the Senate on its 1997 budget on Wednesday, just hours after a new spirit of cooperation had appeared to warm relations with the opposition.

The vote, which was due to take place later in the day, will be the fourth confidence test for Prime Minister Romani Prodi this week in the Senate, where a welter of amendments has put Thursday's deadline for approval by the upper house at risk.

Word of the latest confidence vote tempered enthusiasm that relations between government and opposition could be heading for a thaw following cross-party unity in the lower house on Tuesday night in voting on Italy's broadcasting system.

Prodi's Olive Tree coalition, in office since May, and the media mogul Silvio Berlusconi's centre-right Freedom Alliance bloc voted the same way for the first time in parliament when the Chamber of Deputies approved stop-gap broadcasting measures.
But the budget, centrepiece of Italy's annual legislative diet, has always proved a bitter battleground between the government and the opposition.
Prodi won three confidence votes on the budget held in swift succession on Monday by a mountainous margin after the Freedom Alliance and separatist Northern League boycotted the ballots.
The unusually tough budget aims to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) from the 1997 deficit with much of the emphasis on revenue raising measures including an unpopular "Euro-tax" levy.
Designed to try to squeeze Italy into Europe's planned single currency from the start, the budget must be passed by both houses of parliament by December 31.
The schedule sees the package returning to the Chamber of Deputies for final approval by December 23, a deadline that may require a further confidence vote if it is to be met.

Tuesday's broadcasting vote extends Berlusconi's right to operate three television networks by four months until the end of next May pending fuller legislation, effectively suspending measures that could have put one of his channels off air.

Politicians on both sides of the divide gave a cautious welcome to the cooperative basis of the bill, with some saying the example could bode well for action on vital constitutional reform that has until now hit deadlock.

The broadcasting vote was also the first time that the Communist Refoundation party, whose external support ensures Prodi's majority in the Chamber, had broken ranks with the government. It has branded the measures a gift to Berlusconi.

The opposition, and some forces in the Olive Tree coalition, have voiced deep unease at Prodi's reliance on Communist Refoundation, saying it makes his government hostage to a hardline minority party.

Massimo D'Alema, whose Democratic Party of the Left is the biggest in government, sounded alarm bells this week over the influence of Communist Refoundation and the need for cooperation with the centre-right to break Italy's legislative stall.
The line was echoed on Wednesday by a leading constitutional expert, Giovanni Sartori, who said it was in both blocs' interest to clip Communist Refoundation's wings.

"When you have a real majority, like in England, the government governs and the opposition criticises," Sartori wrote in Corriere della Sera newspaper. "But when there is no real majority then the route of negotiation, agreement and compromise is obligatory."
